4                               ANALYSIS                                  
5        1.   RULING ON DEFENDANT’S MOTION IS PROPER.                     
6        Defendant argues that Schwarzchild v. Tse, 69 F.3d 293 (9th Cir. 1995), proposed that, 
7    prior to provision of class notice and the expiration of the opt-out deadline, an order 
8    compelling arbitration does not bind absent class members (Br. 1 n. 1).  This order holds that it 
9    may exclude from the class definition absent class members who are likely subject to 
10    arbitration, but those excluded persons will not be bound by that ruling and will still be free to 
11    bring suit later and litigate arbitrability issues individually.  Thus, ruling on the motion to 
12    compel arbitration will help fine tune the class.                    
13        2.   CHOICE-OF-LAW.                                              
14        “The choice-of-law inquiry has two levels.  First, we must determine whose choice-of-
15    law rules govern.  Second, applying those rules, we determine whose law applies.”  
16    Schoenberg v. Exportadora de Sal, S.A. de C.V., 930 F.2d 777, 782 (9th Cir. 1991).   
17        Here, the choice-of-law rules of the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws (1969) 
18    govern because there is federal-question jurisdiction in this RICO action.  There is no 
19    California statute on choice-of-law.  See Paulsen v. CNF Inc., 559 F.3d 1061, 1080 (9th Cir. 
20    2009).  So the Restatement requires that this order analyze the factors in Restatement Section 
21    6, as follows:  the interstate system requires that this order apply the proper state substantive 
22    law to each class member to avoid abridging or enlarging rights under 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b); 
23    each state has an interest in applying its laws to its resident class members; and general 
24    contract law will provide some uniformity of result.  Thus, this order shall apply the laws of 
25    the respective class members’ states of residence at the time of purchase.  And, the prior class 
26    certification order justifies the parties’ expectation that this order do so.  
27                                                                         
         3.   LEGAL STANDARDS.                                            
1                                                                         
2        The Federal Arbitration Act states that arbitration agreements “shall be valid, irrevocable, 
3    and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any 
4    contract.”  9 U.S.C. § 2.  “A party seeking to compel arbitration has the burden under the 
5    [Federal Arbitration Act] to show (1) the existence of a valid, written agreement to arbitrate; 
6    and, if it exists, (2) that the agreement to arbitrate encompasses the dispute at issue.”  Ashbey v. 
7    Archstone Prop. Mgmt., Inc., 785 F.3d 1320, 1323 (9th Cir. 2015).  If both questions are 
8    answered in the affirmative, then the [Federal Arbitration Act] requires enforcement of the 
9    arbitration agreement according to its terms.  Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U.S. 
10    213, 218 (1985).  But “[g]enerally applicable contract defenses, such as fraud, duress, or 
11    unconscionability, may be applied to invalidate arbitration agreements without contravening 
12    [the Federal Arbitration Act] § 2.”  Dr.’s Ass’n, Inc. v. Casarotto, 517 U.S. 681, 682 (1996).   
13        In addition, Section 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act provides, in part: 

14             If the making of the arbitration agreement or the failure, neglect, or 
              refusal to perform the same be in issue, the court shall proceed 
15             summarily to the trial thereof.  If no jury trial be demanded by the 
              party alleged to be in default . . . the court shall hear and determine 
16             such issue.                                                 
17    “In applying this language, district courts rely on the summary judgment standard of 
18    [FRCP] 56 . . . .”  Hansen v. LMB Mortg. Servs., Inc., 1 F.4th 667, 670 (9th Cir. 2021).   
19        4.   DEFENDANT HAS NOT MET ITS BURDEN OF PRODUCTION AS TO TEXT-MESSAGE 
              ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS.                                     
20                                                                         
21        Considering the Federal Arbitration Act and the summary judgment rules together, 
22    because the party moving to compel arbitration has the burden of persuasion at trial, the 
23    moving party must first meet its burden of production as to the existence (i.e., formation) of an 
24    arbitration agreement.  See Celotex Corp. v. Cattrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322–23 (1986).  If the 
25    moving party does so, only then must the nonmoving party meet its burden to show a genuine 
26    dispute as to the existence of an arbitration agreement.  Ibid.  Whether an arbitration agreement 
27    exists is for a court to determine.  Three Valleys Mun. Water Dist. v. E.F. Hutton & Co., 925 
1    of material fact as to whether the parties formed an arbitration agreement, the court must 
2    proceed without delay to a trial . . . and hold any motion to compel arbitration in abeyance until 
3    the factual issues have been resolved.”  Hansen, 1 F.4th at 672 (remanding for a trial because 
4    both parties met their respective burdens).  But if the moving party does not meet its initial 
5    burden of production, a district court must deny the motion to compel.  See Houghton v. South, 
6    965 F.2d 1532, 1536–37 (9th Cir. 1992) (reversing grant of summary judgment where movant 
7    did not meet initial burden of production); Hamilton v. Keystone Tankship Corp., 539 F.2d 
8    684, 686 (9th Cir. 1976) (same).                                     
9        Here, defendant has not met its burden of production to show the existence of text-
10    message arbitration agreements under the first exclusion to the class definition.  In its attempt 
11    to do so, defendant has offered several items of evidence.  The Declaration of Luis Fuentes, an 
12    employee of defendant from May 2012 to the present, states that “[defendant]’s policy and 
13    practice was to send service messages affecting all customers, such as notices of updated 
14    Terms and Conditions, to all account owners” (Fuentes Decl. ¶ 5).  Similarly, the Declaration 
15    of Anne-Marie Blandino, an employee of defendant from May 2014 to January 2021, states: 

16                  When [defendant] updates its Terms and Conditions, its 
              custom and practice has been to notify all account owners by text 
17             message.  I have been involved in other text-message campaigns to 
              all [of defendant’s] account owners regarding legal notices and 
18             policy changes.                                             

19                  When [defendant] intended to send legal notices affecting 
              all customers, such as updated Terms and Conditions, [defendant] 
20             would send the text message to all of its account owners using an 
              automated vendor tool (at that time, the Telescope platform). 
21                                                                         
22    (Blandino Decl. ¶¶ 7–8).  Defendant argues these statements establish its routine practice, 
23    supporting that it acted in accordance with this practice on May 22, 2014.  FRE 406.   
24        Further, the Declaration of Luis Fuentes states the following:   

25                  I personally examined the system-generated records in the 
              Telescope platform regarding [text-message] campaigns.      
26             According to those records, a former employee . . . used the 
              Telescope platform to send the text messages in connection with 
27             the May 2014 . . . campaign.                                
                   In July 2015, I used the “Campaign Manager” tool       
1             associated with the Telescope platform to export the system 
              generated records for these text message campaigns.  The data I 
2             exported had been automatically generated and saved by the  
              Telescope platform as text message campaigns were sent.  The 
3             Campaign Manager tool exported the data as a spreadsheet.  This 
              spreadsheet listed each of the data fields available in the platform 
4             associated with the campaigns, including the campaign name, the 
              campaign start date, the campaign creator, the campaign content, 
5             and the recipient count.                                    
6    (Fuentes Decl. ¶¶ 9–10) (cleaned up).  Earlier in this litigation, defendant produced the 
7    spreadsheet referenced in the Fuentes Declaration (Dkt. No. 202-1).  The spreadsheet purports 
8    to show that, of the 3,469,178 accounts owners as of May 2014 (Braxton Decl. ¶ 6), the text 
9    message was sent to 3,437,214 account owners on May 22, 2014 (Dkt. No. 202-1; Fuentes 
10    Decl. ¶ 13).  It also purports to show that, on several occasions thereafter, defendant re-sent the 
11    same text message to a total of 20,324 account owners that did not receive it on May 22, 2014 
12    (Dkt. No. 202-1).  Each account could have had multiple lines of service (i.e., associated phone 
13    numbers) in addition to the account owner’s line (Braxton Decl. ¶ 6).  There were 4,705,834 
14    lines of service as of May 2014 (ibid.).                             
15        Additionally, defendant has provided a list of 379,813 class members who had lines of 
16    service with defendant on May 22, 2014, and whose associated accounts showed payment for 
17    cellular service thereafter (Braxton Decl., Exh. C).  The list includes class members’ names, 
18    account numbers, and states of residence (ibid.).  Defendant argues that those 379,813 class 
19    members must arbitrate.                                              
20        Defendant’s evidence falls short for several reasons.            
21        First, defendant’s evidence of routine practice is inadmissible.  Under FRE 406, 
22    “[e]vidence of a person’s habit or an organization’s routine practice may be admitted to prove 
23    that on a particular occasion the person or organization acted in accordance with the habit or 
24    routine practice.”  But our court of appeals has stated:             

25             [H]abit or pattern of conduct is never to be lightly established, and 
              evidence of examples, for purpose of establishing such habit, is to 
26             be carefully scrutinized before admission . . . .  It is only when the 
              examples offered to establish such pattern of conduct or habit are 
27             “numerous enough to base an inference of systematic conduct” . . . 
1    Mathes v. The Clipper Fleet, 774 F.2d 980, 984 (9th Cir. 1985) (citation omitted).  Here, 
2    neither Fuentes nor Blandino offered any examples establishing defendant’s routine practice.  
3    Moreover, in his deposition, Fuentes could not recall the date of any campaign that sent a text 
4    message to all account owners (Fuentes Dep. 13).  Thus, defendant has not provided examples 
5    “numerous enough to base an inference of systematic conduct.”  Mathes, 774 F.2d at 984. 
6        Second, neither Blandino nor Fuentes has personal knowledge of the text-message 
7    campaign (Blandino Decl. ¶ 4; Fuentes Dep. 45).  Thus, neither Blandino nor Fuentes can 
8    confirm that, on May 22, 2014, defendant adhered to its purported practice of sending such text 
9    messages to all account owners.  Nor does Declarant Braxton have personal knowledge of the 
10    text-message campaign.  He declares merely that he has personal knowledge of class members 
11    associated with active accounts on May 22, 2014, and whose accounts showed payment for 
12    service thereafter (Braxton Decl. ¶ 13).  He does not state that he has personal knowledge of 
13    those who received the text message on May 22, 2014 (see ibid.).  Thus, none of defendant’s 
14    declarants have personal knowledge of the formation of arbitration agreements via text 
15    message on May 22, 2014.                                             
16        Third, other evidence from defendant casts doubt over whether class members actually 
17    received the text message on May 22, 2014.  Defendant previously produced two items of 
18    evidence indicating that former named plaintiff Jermaine Thomas received the text message on 
19    May 22, 2014:  (1) an affidavit of an employee with personal knowledge that Thomas received 
20    the text message (Dkt. No. 50-1); and (2) a list of codes and dates corresponding to text 
21    messages sent to Thomas’ lines of service (Dkt. No. 377-5).  Defendant should have similar 
22    evidence for all class members whom it asserts also received the text message on May 22, 
23    2014.  Defendant’s failure to produce such evidence suggests the class members whom 
24    defendant seeks to exclude did not receive the text message.         
25        Fourth, the spreadsheet referenced in the Fuentes Declaration is inadmissible under the 
26    Best Evidence Rule.  Under FRE 1002, “[a]n original writing, recording, or photograph is 
27    required in order to prove its content unless these rules or a federal statute provides otherwise.”  
1    about the original’s authenticity or the circumstances make it unfair to admit the duplicate.”  
2    FRE 1003.  “A ‘duplicate’ means a counterpart produced by a mechanical, photographic, 
3    chemical, electronic, or other equivalent process or technique that accurately reproduces the 
4    original.”  FRE 1001(e).  There are exceptions to the requirement of an original.  FRE 1004.   
5        The spreadsheet here was proffered to prove its content (that the text-message was sent to 
6    nearly all account owners), but it is not an original.  The spreadsheet contains information 
7    originally stored in a database by a non-party (Fuentes Dep. 27).  Although Declarant Fuentes 
8    “exported the data as a spreadsheet,” suggesting the spreadsheet may be a machine-generated 
9    duplicate, it “[was] not . . . in the format . . . that was downloaded from the campaign tool 
10    manager” (Fuentes Dep. 35).  More importantly, a different employee of defendant manually 
11    added information to the spreadsheet thereafter (Fuentes Decl. ¶ 10; Fuentes Dep. 34–35).  
12    Thus, this order finds the spreadsheet is not a duplicate and is inadmissible.  See U.S. v. Childs, 
13    5 F.3d 1328, 1335 (9th Cir. 1993).                                   
14        Worse yet, the alterations in the spreadsheet were made to indicate whether two specific 
15    customers “received certain campaign messages,” again suggesting that defendant actually 
16    kept records of those who received its text messages (Fuentes Dep. 28).  Defendant’s failure to 
17    produce similar data for the class members it seeks to exclude here suggests that those class 
18    members did not receive the text message on May 22, 2014.            
19        Fifth, defendant did not establish that it had the ability to direct text messages solely to 
20    account owners’ lines of service — as opposed to all lines of service.  Specifically, defendant 
21    argues it sent the text message to over 3.4 million account owners on May 22, 2014, but 
22    Declarant Fuentes testified that he was unaware of any procedure for sending a text message to 
23    only account owners (Fuentes Dep. 20).  Similarly, Declarant Braxton testified that he was 
24    unaware of any data field within defendant’s electronic records that designated an account 
25    owner’s line of service (Braxton Dep. 13).                           
26        Moreover, defendant previously produced a document showing that former plaintiff 
27    Thomas received the text message on May 22, 2014, at two lines of service associated with his 
1    account owners and their associated lines of service may have received the text message.  
2    Those associated lines of service, therefore, would have received text messages that were 
3    meant for unrelated account owners.  Thus, the 3.4 million text messages may have reached 
4    less than 3.4 million account owners.                                
5        To illustrate, for ten account owners with one additional line of service each (twenty total 
6    lines of service), if defendant sent ten text messages, then only five account owners and their 
7    associated lines (ten total lines) would have received a text, leaving five account owners and 
8    their associated lines without having received a text at all.        
9        Defendant has not met its burden of production to show the absence of a genuine dispute 
10    of material fact regarding the existence of text-message arbitration agreements.  The findings 
11    above — that defendant’s evidence of routine practice is inadmissible, defendant’s spreadsheet 
12    regarding the text-message campaign is inadmissible, none of defendant’s declarants have 
13    personal knowledge regarding the text-message campaign, previously produced evidence 
14    suggests class members did not receive the text message, and defendant was unable to send the 
15    text message solely to account owners — demonstrate that fewer than 379,813 class members 
16    whom defendant seeks to exclude actually received the text message of May 22, 2014.  And, 
17    there is no way to determine who received the text message.  Thus, as to the first exclusion 
18    above, defendant’s motion to compel arbitration is DENIED.           
19        5.   ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS BY ELECTRONIC SIGNATURE.             
20             A.   DEFENDANT HAS MET ITS BURDEN OF PRODUCTION.            
21        Defendant argues 15,529 class members agreed to arbitrate via electronic signature under 
22    the second exclusion to the class definition (Braxton Decl. ¶ 16).  To show class members 
23    agreed to arbitrate, defendant cites the Braxton Declaration and proffers copies of invoices 
24    showing 5,622 electronic signatures executed by class members after May 2017.  Plaintiffs 
25    argue that the invoices constitute new evidence, contravening FRCP 26 and FRCP 37.  For that 
26    reason, plaintiffs seek to exclude evidence of the 5,622 electronic signatures. 
27        Defendant has met its burden of production as to the existence of arbitration agreements 
1    defendant, reviewed defendant’s records, and Braxton identified 15,529 class members who, 
2    on or after May 1, 2017, “either returned to [defendant] after having terminated service or who 
3    added a new line of service onto an existing account at a store” (Braxton Decl. ¶ 16).  Exhibit F 
4    to the Braxton Declaration is a list of those class members’ names, states of residence, and 
5    account numbers.  Michael Moses, a retail manager for defendant, declares that those class 
6    members could not have returned or added a new line in-store without executing an electronic 
7    signature:                                                           

8             [I]f a payment terminal did not have the signature capture device, a 
              customer could not add a line or activate a line of service; nor 
9             could they use a credit card for the underlying bill payment.  This 
              measure ensures that all customers are required to accept the 
10             Terms and Conditions after an opportunity to review them when 
              completing a transaction, and the point-of-sale systems prevent a 
11             transaction from being completed unless and until the Terms and 
              Conditions were accepted through completion of a signature  
12             capture.                                                    
13    (Moses Decl. ¶ 10).  Plaintiffs do not dispute that Braxton and Moses have personal knowledge 
14    of those facts, and this order finds no reason to question their knowledge.  Thus, defendant has 
15    met its burden of production to show the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact as to the 
16    existence of arbitration agreements by electronic signature.         
17        Because the Braxton and Moses Declarations are sufficient to meet defendant’s burden of 
18    production, copies of the class members’ electronic signatures are unnecessary to meet that 
19    burden.  Thus, defendant’s failure to produce the electronic signatures during discovery was 
20    “harmless.”  FRCP 37(c).  Defendant may use those records to support the instant motion.   
21        Plaintiffs cite three decisions for the proposition that the Braxton and Moses Declarations 
22    alone are insufficient for defendant to meet its burden of production (Opp. 20).  Those 
23    decisions, however, are distinguishable and unpersuasive.  The plaintiffs in two of those 
24    decisions provided affidavits stating that they did not sign arbitration agreements, but plaintiffs 
25    do not provide any such affidavits here.  Li v. A Perfect Day Franchise, Inc., 281 F.R.D. 373, 
26    384 (N.D. Cal. 2012) (Judge Lucy Koh) (referencing a prior order); Camara v. Mastro’s Rests. 
27    LLC, 952 F.3d 372, 375 (D.C. Cir. 2020).  And, the defendant in the third decision did not 
1    defendant has done so here.  Andreoli v. Youngevity Int’l, Inc., No. 16-CV-02922-BTM-JLB, 
2    2018 WL 1470264, at *6 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 23, 2018) (Judge Barry Moskowitz). 
3        Because plaintiffs do not dispute the personal knowledge of Braxton or Moses, plaintiffs 
4    have not met their burden of production to show a genuine dispute of material fact as to the 
5    existence of arbitration agreements.  Thus, there is an absence of a genuine dispute of material 
6    fact as to the existence of 15,529 arbitration agreements.  Therefore, no trial is necessary as to 
7    this exclusion.                                                      
8             B.   THE ARBITRATION AGREEMENTS ARE VALID.                  
9        “[T]he question ‘who has the primary power to decide arbitrability’ turns upon what the 
10    parties agreed about that matter.”  First Options of Chi., Inc. v. Kaplan, 514 U.S. 938, 943 
11    (1995) (emphasis in original).  “Unless the parties clearly and unmistakably provide otherwise, 
12    the question of whether the parties agreed to arbitrate is to be decided by the court, not the 
13    arbitrator.”  AT & T Techs., Inc. v. Commc’ns Workers of Am., 475 U.S. 643, 649 (1986). 
14        Here, the parties did not “clearly and unmistakably” delegate the issue of validity to an 
15    arbitrator.  Rather, the parties agreed that a court would decide that issue (Dkt. No. 50-32).  
16    Thus, this order shall resolve validity issues.                      
17        Applying California law, our court of appeals has stated the following: 

18             A contract may incorporate documents and terms by reference.  
              Where it is clear that a party is assenting to a contract that 
19             incorporates other documents by reference, the incorporation is 
              valid — and the terms of the incorporated document are binding — 
20             so long as the incorporation is “clear and unequivocal, the 
              reference is called to the attention of the other party and he 
21             consents thereto, and the terms of the incorporated document are 
              known or easily available to the contracting parties.”      
22                                                                         
23    In re Holl, 925 F.3d 1076, 1084 (9th Cir. 2019).  In Holl, the contract referred to separate terms
